summary:
Putrajaya is Malaysia's federal territory and the seat of the federal administration. It stands under the national framework carried by the parent record: the federal Penal Code's offences covering same-sex conduct, the absence of any legal gender-recognition procedure, and the absence of statutory protection against discrimination or hate crime on grounds of gender identity all apply within the territory as they do across Malaysia.

The territory-specific layer is Putrajaya's own Sharia criminal enactment, the instrument it shares with Kuala Lumpur as a federal territory. It reaches same-sex activity and gender nonconformity through cross-dressing provisions and binds Muslims only, so a non-Muslim visitor falls outside its scope while remaining subject to the federal Penal Code.

Neither source records a Putrajaya-specific enforcement case. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, and the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters release of 10 August 2022 document no raid, arrest or prosecution inside the territory; the second source states this explicitly. The absence of a recorded case in these two sources is not evidence that the provisions stand unused.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement of the same federal offences is documented elsewhere in Malaysia since the 2018 election, which indicates what the territory's own provisions could be used for: an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur in which at least 20 LGBT people were arrested; an August raid on an LGBT venue in which twenty men were arrested, with no year given in the source; a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned; and November 2023 plans in Johor for conversion-therapy centres. Every one of these cases sits in another jurisdiction, and none is attributed to Putrajaya.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters reported on 10 August 2022 that 73 LGBT people were interviewed across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 for a report on conversion practices, discrimination and violence, and that government-run rehabilitation programmes had drawn at least 1,733 participants as of June 2021. The population surveyed is LGBT people nationally rather than Putrajaya residents, and the fieldwork window closed in 2021.
localsOnly:
Residents of Putrajaya who are Muslim are bound by the federal territory's Sharia enactment, which criminalises same-sex activity and cross-dressing; non-Muslim residents fall outside its scope but remain subject to the federal Penal Code. Enforcement of Sharia offences in the federal territories is carried out by Islamic religious authorities rather than the police.

Residents have no route to a legal change of gender marker: the sources record no gender-recognition procedure in Malaysia. They also have no statutory protection against dismissal, denial of health care or other discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime provision covering such conduct.

Government-run rehabilitation and conversion programmes are available to residents and had drawn at least 1,733 participants nationally as of June 2021, according to the Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters release of 10 August 2022; the sources give no figure for Putrajaya alone.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Putrajaya-specific enforcement, prosecution or incident data appears in either source. Whether the federal territory's Sharia enactment has been amended, or has been used in any recent proceeding, is not sourced here.

The Human Dignity Trust profile is a national country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, and its enforcement examples are drawn from other Malaysian jurisdictions; it records no case in Putrajaya.

The Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters release of 10 August 2022 reports fieldwork conducted between 2018 and 2021 and states that no Putrajaya-specific enforcement case is documented. Its figures therefore describe LGBT people nationally over a window that closed in 2021, not current conditions in the territory.

The source gives no year for the August raid on an LGBT venue in which twenty men were arrested, so its date remains unresolved.

Whether the federal Penal Code penalties stated in the sources apply in Putrajaya without local variation is carried by the parent record rather than established here.
